editions.label: DAILY EDITION
editions.title: Three things worth knowing
editions.subtitle: Stronger medical-device quality checks, a more comprehensive genetic test and temporary classrooms restoring education after floods.

stories.title: WHO expanded quality checks for essential medical devices
stories.text: WHO expanded its prequalification programme to cover a wider range of products, including male and female condoms, intrauterine devices and AI-assisted tuberculosis-screening software. The programme independently assesses quality, safety and performance, then lists products that meet its standards for procurement guidance.
stories.why: The expansion can help countries with limited regulatory capacity identify trustworthy devices for reproductive health, HIV prevention and earlier TB screening. It does not automatically make products available: manufacturers must apply, devices must pass assessment, and procurement and delivery still have to follow.

stories.title: One DNA test diagnosed more than a third of long-unsolved muscle-disease cases
stories.text: Researchers applied a targeted long-read DNA test to 53 Australians with known or suspected inherited muscle disease. It produced new diagnoses for 11 of 31 people whose earlier genetic testing had not found a cause, while examining more than 300 disease-linked genes in one assay.
stories.why: A confirmed diagnosis can guide monitoring, family counselling, support and eligibility for clinical trials while replacing multiple separate genetic tests. This was a small Australian research cohort; the test is not yet routine care and it does not treat or cure the diseases.

stories.title: Temporary classrooms returned more than 1,400 children to learning after Nepal’s floods
stories.text: UNICEF, Nepal’s government and partners established 48 temporary learning centres after floods disrupted education for more than 14,000 children across 62 schools and learning sites. The centres have helped over 1,400 children resume lessons, with learning materials and psychosocial support.
stories.why: Restoring school gives children routine, support and continuity after a devastating disaster. The response currently reaches only a fraction of affected pupils; many families remain displaced, access is blocked in some areas and substantial rebuilding is still required.

editions.label: DAILY EDITION
editions.title: Three things worth knowing
editions.subtitle: A newly identified genetic disorder, a renewable-energy record in Australia and new finance for sustainable cities.

stories.title: Researchers identified a rare genetic cause of a neurodevelopmental disorder
stories.text: Researchers found the same overactive BMPR2 variant in six unrelated children, five of whom had global developmental delay and four an autism diagnosis. Fruit-fly experiments showed that the variant drove excessive developmental signalling, while two experimental compounds reduced that signalling in isolated fly tissue.
stories.why: The finding can give some families a biological explanation and a clearer direction for future treatment research. It is based on only six children and fly models; the compounds are research tools, not treatments ready for patients.

stories.title: Solar and wind supplied a record 80.4% of demand on Australia’s main grid
stories.text: For one 30-minute period, sunshine and wind met 80.4% of electricity demand across Australia’s national electricity market. Rooftop solar alone supplied more than half, supported by utility-scale solar, wind and a small amount of hydro.
stories.why: The milestone shows how far a large power system can move toward renewable electricity as generation and storage expand. It was a brief record during sunny, low-demand conditions; renewables averaged 44% over the year to June, and investment remains below the pace needed for the 2030 target.

stories.title: A €50 million guarantee will help finance sustainable cities in developing countries
stories.text: The European Union is providing the UN Capital Development Fund with a guarantee of up to €50 million to help attract public and private finance for urban infrastructure in least-developed countries, small island states and fragile settings.
stories.why: The facility can reduce financing risks for projects such as clean energy, water, transport, housing, education and healthcare where conventional capital is scarce. It is a guarantee rather than €50 million of direct project spending, and the amount of additional finance and infrastructure ultimately delivered is not yet known.

editions.label: DAILY EDITION
editions.title: Three things worth knowing
editions.subtitle: Real-world lessons for incisionless cancer care, a second Sihek release and $115 million returning to delivery workers.

stories.title: An incisionless liver-tumour treatment showed low procedural toxicity in real-world use
stories.text: A review of 972 US patients treated with histotripsy found that 88.4% went home the same day, while acute kidney injury occurred in 1.2%, readmission in 0.9% and emergency visits in 0.4%. The outpatient procedure uses focused sound waves rather than an incision to destroy tumour tissue.
stories.why: The results suggest this newer treatment can often be delivered with few immediate procedural complications. The study was retrospective and could not assess tumour control or causation; 11.1% of patients died within 30 days, underscoring the need for better patient selection and prospective evidence.

stories.title: Up to eight extinct-in-the-wild Sihek are preparing for release
stories.text: Ten Sihek, also known as Guam kingfishers, are entering a two-month quarantine ahead of a planned release on predator-free Palmyra Atoll. Up to eight could join the nine birds released there in 2024, nearly doubling the species’ wild population.
stories.why: A second release could strengthen the foundation for a self-sustaining wild population of a species with fewer than 150 birds left worldwide. The birds must first clear quarantine, and although wild pairs have nested and laid eggs, none has hatched yet.

stories.title: More than $115 million will be returned to New York delivery workers
stories.text: A $131.5 million settlement requires DoorDash to pay more than $115 million in restitution to over 260,000 delivery workers after a city investigation found minimum-pay and missed-payment violations. Eligible workers will not need to file a claim.
stories.why: The settlement turns worker-protection rules into direct compensation and includes more than $16 million in penalties and fees. Payments will vary by worker and are scheduled in stages beginning in late October, with a smaller second round in early 2027.
stories.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection · 22 Sep 2026

editions.label: DAILY EDITION
editions.title: Three things worth knowing
editions.subtitle: Promising diabetes trial results, a new limit for complex life and lower trade barriers between the EU and the Philippines.

stories.title: An experimental diabetes drug delivered strong blood-sugar and weight results
stories.text: In a 447-person Phase II trial, the highest dose of Roche’s once-weekly enicepatide lowered average HbA1c by 2.65 percentage points and body weight by 15.5% after 48 weeks. Sixty-two percent of participants at that dose reached blood-sugar levels below the diabetes range.
stories.why: The results point to another potentially effective option for people living with type 2 diabetes and obesity. The figures are company-reported topline data, however, and the drug still needs larger late-stage trials to confirm long-term benefits and safety.

stories.title: A newly described amoeba has raised the heat limit for complex life
stories.text: Scientists found that Incendiamoeba cascadensis can reproduce at 63°C, three degrees above the previous known upper limit for eukaryotes, and remain active at 64°C. It also recovered after five minutes at 70°C.
stories.why: The discovery expands what scientists know about where complex cells can survive and may inform biotechnology and the search for life beyond Earth. It does not show that similar life exists elsewhere, and the amoeba still depends on a very specific ecosystem.

stories.title: The EU and the Philippines reached an initial deal to remove most tariffs
stories.text: The two sides politically approved the key terms of a trade agreement that would eliminate tariffs on more than 94% of goods. Their existing bilateral trade totals €17.6 billion in goods and €10.3 billion in services.
stories.why: Lower barriers could expand trade, investment and market access across both economies. The agreement is not yet final: its terms must still be turned into legal text and complete the required approval processes.

editions.label: DAILY EDITION
editions.title: Three things worth knowing
editions.subtitle: Preclinical lung imaging, clean-energy access in Nigeria and renewed Amazon restoration.

stories.title: An experimental MRI agent found 1-millimetre lung tumours in animals
stories.text: A protein-based contrast agent called hProCA32.Collagen2 identified lung tumours and metastases as small as 1 millimetre in animal studies, while mapping collagen associated with aggressive disease.
stories.why: Earlier, radiation-free imaging could widen treatment options, but this is preclinical evidence and the agent still needs to prove safe and effective in people.
stories.source: Reuters, reporting a Science Advances study · 16 Sep 2026

stories.title: A $300 million fund is moving Nigerian off-grid power into deployment
stories.text: The Nigeria Distributed Renewable Energy Fund has commercially launched to finance mini-grids, standalone solar and other distributed power. The World Bank says its initial IDA contribution is $25 million.
stories.why: Dedicated capital can help electricity reach underserved communities, although the real impact will depend on which projects are financed and how many connections are delivered.
stories.source: Africa50, with NSIA, SEforALL and World Bank Group · 20 Sep 2026

stories.title: New finance could extend an Amazon restoration effort that has planted nearly 15 million trees
stories.text: Mombak secured the first close of a second reforestation fund targeting $150 million, plus access to a 200-million-real credit line. Its first fund financed restoration across 15 Amazon farms where nearly 15 million native trees were planted.
stories.why: More finance can restore additional degraded land, but the new fund has not reached its final close and carbon removals should complement—not replace—direct emissions cuts.
